metadata.note: The Florida Railroad -- Gainesville's first railroad and the first line to link Florida's Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Chartered in 1853, David Levy Yulee's road reached Gainesville from Fernandina in 1859 and Cedar Key in 1861; part of the Gainesville depot built around 1860 still stands, one of only three pre-Civil-War depots left in the state. The line passed to the Seaboard Air Line, which stopped running passenger trains through the Gainesville station somewhere between 1932 and 1938 and abandoned the Cedar Key Subdivision in 1932. Gainesville's last passenger trains of any kind ran in 1971, and the city was not among those Amtrak kept on May 1 that year -- it has had no passenger rail since, only an Amtrak Thruway bus from Jacksonville.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Only the Fernandina-Gainesville half of this railroad is drawn; the Cedar Key half southwest of Gainesville could not be traced, and the intermediate opening dates along the line are not established, so the whole drawn extent appears at once in 1859. The end of Seaboard passenger service at Gainesville is sourced only as a range, 'between 1932 and 1938', and 1938 is used. Headways are estimates throughout. STILL MISSING FOR GAINESVILLE: the Atlantic Coast Line route through the city (its Main Street line was replaced in 1948) and the Tampa and Jacksonville Railway south to Micanopy -- the 1971 end of Gainesville passenger service belongs to one of those, not to this line. Neither could be traced: OpenStreetMap has no continuous right-of-way from Gainesville toward Archer, Hawthorne or Micanopy.

properties.geometry_source: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via Overpass. Fernandina to Waldo follows the active CSX line; Waldo to Gainesville follows the abandoned right-of-way OSM still labels 'Florida Railroad', continuing onto the Waldo Road Greenway and the Downtown Connector Rail-Trail into Gainesville. Routing was restricted to abandoned right-of-way and rail-trails on the southern leg, because the active subdivisions near Gainesville (Deerhaven, Wildwood) head elsewhere and an unrestricted shortest path diverted onto them.
properties.geometry_quality: 723 points, 104.4 mi against the 99 miles the company's own station table gives for Fernandina to Gainesville. Quality measured as synthetic connector content rather than vertex spacing, because this line runs dead straight for miles at a time and sparse vertices there are correct: 17% of the drawn length (17.9 mi across 135 places) is straight-line connector I inserted where the mapped right-of-way breaks; the other 83% sits on mapped ways. The breaks concentrate on the Waldo–Gainesville leg, where the line was lifted and only fragments survive — that leg alone is about 25% connector. LATER ALIGNMENT: drawn on what survives today, not a verified 1859 alignment. NOT DRAWN: everything southwest of Gainesville — Archer, Bronson, Otter Creek, Cedar Key — no continuous right-of-way is mapped and no path resolved. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 2 ruled segments totalling 42 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: Chartered by the Florida Legislature in 1853 to run from Fernandina on the Atlantic to Cedar Key on the Gulf, David Levy Yulee's Florida Railroad reached Gainesville in 1859 -- the town's first railroad, and part of the first line to connect Florida's east and west coasts once it was completed to Cedar Key in 1861. Part of the Gainesville depot dates from about 1860 and is one of only three Florida depots surviving from before the Civil War. The war hit the line hard: the USS Hatteras raided Cedar Key in January 1862 and a Union squadron seized Fernandina that March. The Cedar Key half southwest of Gainesville is not drawn -- see geometry_quality. Frequency estimated/unsourced

segments.note: Under the Seaboard Air Line from 1900 the old Florida Railroad north of Waldo became part of the Ocala District, with Baldwin-Waldo forming SAL main line. The Gainesville depot was remodelled between 1892 and 1897 to give two passenger waiting rooms, one for whites and one for blacks, and a new passenger depot with segregated waiting rooms followed in 1910. Between 1932 and 1938 the Seaboard stopped running passenger trains through the Gainesville station, including the Waldo-Tampa service, and it abandoned the Cedar Key Subdivision in 1932. The end year used here is the later bound of that 1932-1938 range. Frequency estimated/unsourced
